How does ArrayList grow? What is the default capacity?

A no-arg ArrayList begins with a shared empty array and allocates 10 slots on the first add. When full, new capacity is old + (old >> 1), or 1.5 times, and elements are copied with System.arraycopy. Observed capacities: 10, 15, 22, 33. Adds are amortized O(1) because the growth is geometric. Pre-size if you know the count.
Predict the output. List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3, 4)); list.remove(1); list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1)); System.out.println(list);
[3, 4]. remove(1) with an int picks remove(int index) and removes the value 2. remove(Integer) picks remove(Object) and removes the value 1. Overload resolution prefers no boxing.
Predict the output. var list = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b", "c")); for (String s : list) if (s.equals("b")) list.remove(s); System.out.println(list);

[a, c], with no exception. "b" is second-to-last. After removal, size is 2 and the iterator's cursor is 2, so hasNext() returns false and next(), which contains the modCount check, is never called. Remove "a" or "c" instead, and you get ConcurrentModificationException.
Predict the output. Set<Short> set = new HashSet<>(); for (short i = 0; i < 5; i++) { set.add(i); set.remove(i - 1); } System.out.println(set.size());

5. i - 1 is an int, so it boxes to Integer. remove(Object) accepts it, but an Integer never equals a Short, so nothing is removed. The same trap: List<Long>.contains(1) is false, and contains(1L) is true.
What does subList return? What can go wrong?

A view on the parent list. Non-structural and structural changes through the view pass to the parent. A structural change on the parent after creating the view makes later view calls throw ConcurrentModificationException. Retaining a small sublist also keeps the entire parent array alive. Copy it when you need independence.

Why is LinkedList usually slower than ArrayList even for insertions?

Getting to position i takes O(n) pointer hops, each a likely cache miss, since nodes are scattered in memory. ArrayList does an O(n) shift, too, but as one fast bulk memory move in contiguous memory. LinkedList also allocates a node per element, adding GC pressure. LinkedList's O(1) advantage holds only at the ends, where ArrayDeque is better, or when you already have an iterator at the position.
Why should you prefer ArrayDeque over Stack and LinkedList?

Stack extends synchronized Vector, paying for locks you rarely need, and exposes index methods that break LIFO. LinkedList allocates a node per element. ArrayDeque is a circular array with amortized O(1) at both ends and good locality. It forbids nulls, and iterates from the head, so a stack built with push iterates top-first.
How does PriorityQueue work? Is printing it sorted?

It is a binary heap in an array. Parent at (i-1)/2, children at 2i+1 and 2i+2. Add sifts up, and poll moves the last element to the root and sifts down, both O(log n). Printing shows array order, which is not sorted: inserting 5,1,4,2,3 prints [1, 2, 4, 5, 3]. Only polling returns sorted order: 12345.

Why does HashMap XOR the hash with its upper 16 bits?

The index comes from only the low bits (hash & (n-1)). Hash codes that differ only in high bits, such as Floats or shifted keys, would all land in the same bin. h ^ (h >>> 16) mixes the high half into the low half. It is one cheap operation, since tree bins already handle the worst cases.
Why must the table size be a power of two? What happens with new HashMap<>(17)?

So that hash & (n-1) equals a non-negative modulo, using a fast mask, and so that resizing can split each bin by a single bit. The constructor rounds up: 17 gives 32, allocated at the first put. A downside is that weak hash functions are exposed, which is why the bits are spread.
When exactly does a bin treeify? Is it at 8 nodes?

The check fires while appending to a list that already has 8 nodes, so the conversion happens when the 9th node arrives, and only if the table has at least 64 slots. If it is smaller, the map doubles instead. Verified on Java 21 by reflection with keys that have the same hash: from capacity 64, the 9th key created TreeNodes. From capacity 16, the 9th key resized to 32, the 10th to 64, and the 11th treeified.
What happens during resize? Does it recompute hashCode?

No. Each node stores its hash. Doubling adds one index bit. Each bin splits into a lo list staying at j and a hi list moving to j + oldCap, based on hash & oldCap. Relative order is kept. Resizing is O(n), so pre-size large maps. It also never shrinks automatically: removing all entries leaves a big table, and iteration stays proportional to capacity.
Why was HashMap dangerous under concurrency in Java 7, and is it safe in Java 8?

Java 7 used head insertion during transfer, reversing lists. Two threads resizing together could form a circular list, so get hung at 100% CPU. Java 8's tail insertion with lo/hi splitting removes that specific failure, but HashMap is still unsafe: lost updates, wrong size, and corrupted tree bins remain possible. Use ConcurrentHashMap.
Can two unequal objects have the same hashCode? What happens if hashCode returns a constant?

Yes, that is a collision; "Aa" and "BB" both hash to 2112. A constant hashCode is legal and the map still works correctly, but everything lands in one bin: O(n) with a list, O(log n) once it is a tree. If keys are not Comparable, tree lookups may need to search both subtrees, so they degrade further.
What happens if you override equals but not hashCode?

Equal objects get different identity hashes, so they usually go to different bins. map.get(equalKey) returns null, and a HashSet holds duplicates. If you override hashCode only, two objects share a bin but equals (identity) says they differ, so duplicates remain.
Predict the output. var set = new HashSet<List<Integer>>(); var list = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1)); set.add(list); list.add(2); System.out.println(set.contains(list) + " " + set.size());
false 1. A list's hashCode depends on its elements. After the change, contains looks in a different bin. The element remains in the old bin, unreachable by lookup.
Is get returning null proof that a key is absent? What does {null=2, a=null} teach?

No. HashMap allows one null key (hash 0, bin 0) and null values. So get("a") and get("zz") both return null while containsKey differs. getOrDefault and putIfAbsent treat null values differently from each other too: putIfAbsent replaces a null value, whereas getOrDefault returns the stored null.
How would you implement a HashMap from scratch?
Implement an LRU cache without LinkedHashMap, with O(1) get and put.
How does LinkedHashMap maintain order? What does accessOrder do?

It extends HashMap, and entries have before and after links. accessOrder=true moves an entry to the tail on get and put. Overriding removeEldestEntry gives eviction. In access order, get counts as a structural change, so for (k : map.keySet()) map.get(k) throws CME.
Does re-inserting a key change LinkedHashMap's insertion order?
No. Put a=1, b=2, a=3 yields {a=3, b=2}. Since Java 21, putLast and putFirst reposition a key explicitly.
How does TreeMap decide keys are equal?
Only by compareTo or compare returning 0. equals and hashCode are unused. With a length comparator, put("aa", 1); put("bb", 2); prints {aa=2}: the original key remains, and the value is replaced.
Predict the sizes. new HashSet<>(List.of(new BigDecimal("1.0"), new BigDecimal("1.00"))).size(); new TreeSet<>(List.of(new BigDecimal("1.0"), new BigDecimal("1.00"))).size();
2 and 1. BigDecimal.equals considers scale, so the HashSet keeps both. compareTo ignores scale, so the TreeSet sees one value.
What is a red-black tree, and why is it used in TreeMap and HashMap?

A self-balancing BST with colour rules that keep the height at about 2 log₂ n, with few rotations per update. It offers guaranteed O(log n). HashMap uses it for overflowing bins, and TreeMap as its main structure. A plain BST degrades to a linked list on sorted input; red-black trees do not.
Give a use for floorEntry or ceilingEntry.

Tiered pricing: tiers.floorEntry(quantity).getValue() finds the band a quantity falls in. A consistent hash ring: ring.ceilingEntry(hash) finds the next node clockwise, wrapping with firstEntry(). In both, a TreeMap replaces a chain of if-statements or a linear scan.
How is HashSet implemented? Why does add return a boolean?

It wraps a HashMap, using elements as keys and a shared static dummy object as the value. add returns true if map.put returned null, that is, if the key is new. The dummy exists so that put returns non-null for an existing key.
Why use EnumSet instead of HashSet of enum?

It is a bit vector, one long for up to 64 constants. Operations become bit operations, there is no hashing or per-element node, and iteration is in declaration order. It is also more readable than integer flags: EnumSet.of(READ, WRITE).
How does IdentityHashMap differ from HashMap?

It compares keys by reference (==) with System.identityHashCode, and it uses linear probing in a flat array with keys and values in alternate slots. So it violates the Map contract on purpose. Use it for tracking object identity, as in graph copying and cycle detection. Two new String("a") keys are two entries.
When would a WeakHashMap entry never get removed?

When the key stays strongly reachable: a string literal, a key still referenced elsewhere, or a value that references the key. The map holds values strongly, so a value pointing to its key keeps it alive forever. Also, stale entries are purged only when the map is used.
How does ConcurrentHashMap achieve thread safety in Java 8+? How is it different from Java 7?

Java 7 used 16 (by default) Segment locks, each with its own table. Java 8 has one table: reads use volatile access with no lock, empty bins are filled by CAS, and occupied bins are locked with synchronized on the first node. Resize is shared between threads through forwarding nodes. Counting is striped. Long bins become TreeBins.
Is this thread-safe? ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer> m = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); if (!m.containsKey(k)) m.put(k, 1); else m.put(k, m.get(k) + 1);
No. Each call is atomic, but the sequence is check-then-act. Two threads can read the same value and lose an increment. Use m.merge(k, 1, Integer::sum). For very hot counters, use LongAdder values.
Why doesn't ConcurrentHashMap allow null?

Null would be ambiguous. In a HashMap you can follow a null get with containsKey, but concurrently the state may change between calls. Forbidding it means that get returning null always means "not present at that moment". Doug Lea has also said that nulls in maps invite errors in general.
Is ConcurrentHashMap.size() accurate? Can an iterator miss updates?

While writers are active, it is an estimate. Use it for monitoring, not logic. mappingCount() avoids int overflow. Iterators are weakly consistent: they reflect the state at some point at or after creation, never throw CME, and may or may not show concurrent changes.
Predict the result. var m = new ConcurrentHashMap<Integer, Integer>(); m.computeIfAbsent(1, k -> m.computeIfAbsent(1, j -> 2));

On Java 21 it throws IllegalStateException: Recursive update. Older versions could hang (notably Java 8). A mapping function must never update the same map. The HashMap version with an inner put throws ConcurrentModificationException.
Hashtable vs synchronizedMap vs ConcurrentHashMap under load?

The first two use one lock for the entire map, so all threads queue up, even for reads. ConcurrentHashMap lets reads run without locks and writers proceed in parallel on different bins, so throughput scales with cores. Atomic compound methods exist on it. A synchronizedMap iteration needs a manual lock for its whole duration; a ConcurrentHashMap iteration needs none.
When is CopyOnWriteArrayList a bad choice?

With frequent writes or large lists: each write copies the whole array, costing O(n) and much garbage. It suits small, read-mostly lists such as listener registrations. Iterators see an old snapshot, which can be stale, and they do not support remove.
Predict the output. var cow = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2)); for (int x : cow) cow.add(x + 10); System.out.println(cow);
[1, 2, 11, 12]. The loop iterates over the array at the moment it began. With a normal ArrayList, this would throw CME. And there is no infinite loop.
Why is there no ConcurrentTreeMap?

A red-black rebalance changes several nodes at once near the root, so it is hard to make non-blocking without a global lock. Skip list updates are local and can be done by CAS. The result, ConcurrentSkipListMap, is sorted and scales well. It uses more memory and has slower constant factors than a TreeMap in single-threaded use.
ArrayBlockingQueue vs LinkedBlockingQueue?

ArrayBlockingQueue is always bounded, preallocates its array, and uses one lock, so puts and takes contend. LinkedBlockingQueue uses two locks, so producers and consumers can run in parallel. It allocates a node per element and is effectively unbounded unless given a capacity. Choose ArrayBlockingQueue for stable memory and strict limits, or LinkedBlockingQueue(capacity) for throughput.
What is SynchronousQueue, and why does newCachedThreadPool use it?

It has no storage: an insert waits for a matching remove. A ThreadPoolExecutor adds a new thread only when its queue refuses a task. Since offer fails unless a worker is already waiting, tasks go to an idle worker or else create a thread. This gives instant dispatch but unbounded thread growth under load.
What is the difference between add, offer and put? remove, poll, take?
add and remove throw on failure (IllegalStateException, NoSuchElementException). offer and poll return false or null. put and take block. Only BlockingQueues have put and take.
How is fail-fast implemented? Is CME guaranteed?

Using a modCount incremented on structural changes, and expectedModCount in the iterator, checked in next(). It is not guaranteed: it is unsynchronized, and the docs say it is best effort, for bug detection only. set and replacing a map value do not trigger it. For example, map.put(existingKey, v) during iteration of a HashMap is fine.

What does a ListIterator let you do? Predict the output. var li = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b")).listIterator(); li.next(); li.add("x"); li.next(); li.set("B"); while (li.hasPrevious()) System.out.print(li.previous());
Bxa. After next (a), add inserts x before the cursor. The next call returns b, and set replaces it with B. Going backward gives B, x, a.
What is a Spliterator, and why does ArrayList parallelize better than LinkedList?

It is an iterator that can split its source for parallel work, and reports traits such as SIZED and ORDERED. ArrayList's trySplit computes a midpoint in O(1) and gives balanced halves. LinkedList has to walk nodes and copies batches to an array, so splitting is costly and unbalanced.
What is wrong with (a, b) -> a - b as a comparator?

Overflow: Integer.MIN_VALUE - 1 wraps to 2147483647. The result claims MIN_VALUE is greater. It breaks transitivity and can trigger "Comparison method violates its general contract!". Use Integer.compare or Comparator.comparingInt.

Which sort does Java use, and why are there two?
Primitives use dual-pivot quicksort (fast, in place, with stability meaningless). Objects use TimSort (stable, adaptive, fewer comparisons, O(n) on sorted data). parallelSort uses Fork/Join merging.
Arrays.asList vs List.of vs new ArrayList<>(…)?

Arrays.asList: fixed size, set allowed, writes through to the array, allows nulls. List.of: immutable, no nulls, contains(null) throws NPE. new ArrayList<>(…): a fully mutable independent copy. Arrays.asList(int[]) gives a list with a single element, the array itself.
Is Collections.unmodifiableList immutable?

No. It is a read-only view. Anyone with the original reference can change it, and the view shows that. For a true snapshot, use List.copyOf. In a getter, returning an unmodifiable view is a reasonable way to prevent changes while avoiding copying, if the changing visibility is acceptable.
stream.toList() vs collect(Collectors.toList())?

toList() (Java 16) returns an unmodifiable list and allows nulls. Collectors.toList() gives an unspecified mutable list, an ArrayList today. Replacing one by the other can cause UnsupportedOperationException if code later adds to the result.
What did sequenced collections add in Java 21?

Three interfaces: SequencedCollection, SequencedSet and SequencedMap, giving uniform getFirst, getLast, addFirst, addLast, removeFirst, removeLast and reversed. reversed() is a live view. Existing types were adjusted, and LinkedHashSet finally got a way to reach its last element. Sorted collections reject addFirst with UOE. Note that adding reversed and getFirst can conflict with same-named methods in your own List subclasses.
Do these print true? new ArrayList<>(List.of(1)).equals(new LinkedList<>(List.of(1))); new HashSet<>(List.of(1)).equals(new TreeSet<>(List.of(1))); List.of(1).equals(Set.of(1));
true, true, false. The List contract defines equals by elements in order, regardless of implementation, and Set by elements. A List never equals a Set.

Scenario: a service's HashMap cache keeps growing and memory rises. How do you diagnose and fix it?

- Take a heap dump and check the dominators in Eclipse MAT. An unbounded HashMap shows up with a huge retained size.
- Check for keys that never repeat, or mutable keys, which strand entries.
- Replace it with a bounded cache: Caffeine with maximumSize and expireAfterWrite, and hit-rate metrics.
- If shared between threads, also check for data races on the plain HashMap.
Scenario: you need a thread-safe top-N leaderboard with many score updates and reads of the top entries. What would you use?

Use a ConcurrentHashMap<PlayerId, Score> for current scores, and a ConcurrentSkipListSet<ScoreEntry> sorted by score then ID, so that first() and an iterator give the top N. An update removes the old entry and inserts the new one; lock per player or use compute on the map to keep the two structures in step. ScoreEntry must be immutable, and its comparator must include the ID, or equal scores would collapse. At scale, use a Redis sorted set.
Scenario: 10 million lookups per second by integer ID on a read-only dataset of 5 million entries. Is HashMap right?

HashMap would box every key, add one node per entry, and scatter memory. That costs tens of bytes per entry and many cache misses. Better: if IDs are dense, a plain array indexed by ID. Otherwise a sorted int[] with Arrays.binarySearch, or a primitive open-addressing map from a library such as fastutil. Benchmark with JMH using realistic keys. For reads only, immutability removes any need for synchronization.
putIfAbsent vs computeIfAbsent: which is right for a cache?

computeIfAbsent. putIfAbsent(k, expensive()) evaluates its argument before the call, so the expensive work runs on every hit. computeIfAbsent calls the function only on a miss. On a ConcurrentHashMap, it does so atomically, at most once per key, while it holds the bin lock, so the function should be short and must not modify the same map. putIfAbsent also returns the previous value (null on insert), while computeIfAbsent returns the current value, which is what makes the computeIfAbsent(k, x -> new ArrayList<>()).add(v) idiom work. For production caches with eviction and TTL, use Caffeine.
What happens when the remapping function of merge or compute returns null?

The entry is removed. This is deliberate, and it is a neat way to keep counters clean: counts.merge(k, -1, (a, b) -> a + b == 0 ? null : a + b) removes the key when the count reaches zero. However, merge's value argument cannot be null (NPE). computeIfAbsent returning null simply stores nothing. Because ConcurrentHashMap forbids null values, these methods are its only way to express "remove if...".
How do you use a composite key, such as (customerId, date), in a HashMap?

Use a record: record DayKey(long customerId, LocalDate date) {}. It gets value-based equals/hashCode automatically, it is immutable, and it is clearer than concatenating strings such as id + "_" + date, which is slower and can produce ambiguous keys. Make sure the components are themselves immutable with proper equals. A record holding a mutable List or an array does not work well as a key: arrays use identity equality, and a list that changes after insertion changes the hash.
What is the most efficient way to iterate over a Map's keys and values?

Iterate entrySet(), or call map.forEach((k, v) -> ...). Looping over keySet() and calling get(k) for each key does a second hash lookup per entry, and for a TreeMap that is an extra O(log n) each time. To update values in place, use entry.setValue(...) or map.replaceAll(...). To remove entries, use map.entrySet().removeIf(...) or map.values().removeIf(...), never map.remove inside a for-each.

When would you use a BitSet?

A BitSet stores booleans as bits in a long[]. Ten million flags take about 1.25 MB, compared with tens of MB for a Set<Integer> or a boolean[] of 10 MB. It supports fast bulk and/or/xor/andNot, cardinality() and nextSetBit. Typical uses are a Sieve of Eratosthenes, "which IDs in a dense range have we seen", permission masks, and Bloom filters. It is not thread-safe, and it suits dense, non-negative integer ranges. For enum flags, use EnumSet, which works the same way internally.
HashMap vs LinkedHashMap vs TreeMap: which map do you choose?

| HashMap | LinkedHashMap | TreeMap
Iteration order | None you can rely on | Insertion order (or access order) | Sorted by key
get / put | O(1) average | O(1) average | O(log n)
Null key | One allowed | One allowed | No, with natural ordering (NPE)
Key needs | equals and hashCode | equals and hashCode | compareTo or a Comparator
Extra features | None | LRU via removeEldestEntry | Range queries: floorKey, headMap, subMap
Memory | Lowest | Two extra links per entry | Tree node per entry
Rule of thumb: HashMap by default; LinkedHashMap when output order must match input order (JSON, reports) or for a simple LRU; TreeMap when you need sorted keys or "nearest key" lookups. The same choice applies to HashSet, LinkedHashSet and TreeSet, which are built on these maps.
PriorityQueue vs TreeSet vs a sorted ArrayList: how do you keep things in order?

| PriorityQueue | TreeSet | Sorted ArrayList
Duplicates | Allowed | Dropped (when compare returns 0) | Allowed
Insert | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(n) (binary search, then shift)
Smallest element | peek O(1), poll O(log n) | first / pollFirst O(log n) | get(0) O(1)
Largest element | O(n) scan | last O(log n) | O(1)
contains / remove(x) | O(n) | O(log n) | O(log n) / O(n)
Iteration sorted | No | Yes | Yes
Rule of thumb: PriorityQueue when you only ever take the next item (schedulers, top-K, Dijkstra). TreeSet when you need both ends, range queries or fast removal of arbitrary elements, and no duplicates. A sorted list fits data that is built once and then read many times.
synchronizedList vs CopyOnWriteArrayList vs ConcurrentLinkedQueue: which thread-safe list-like structure?

| Collections.synchronizedList | CopyOnWriteArrayList | ConcurrentLinkedQueue
Locking | One lock for every call | Lock-free reads; writes take a lock and copy the array | Lock-free (CAS)
Write cost | Normal | O(n) per write | O(1)
Iteration | Must wrap in synchronized (list), else CME is possible | Snapshot: never throws CME, misses later writes | Weakly consistent, never throws CME
Index access | Yes | Yes | No: FIFO only; size() is O(n)
Best for | Low contention, simple code | Many reads, rare writes (listeners, config) | Producer/consumer without blocking
Rule of thumb: if threads hand work to each other, use a queue (a BlockingQueue if consumers should wait). If the list is read far more than written, use CopyOnWriteArrayList. Compound actions such as "check then add" need extra locking with any of them.
Array vs ArrayList: when is a plain array the better choice?

| Array (int[], String[]) | ArrayList<E>
Size | Fixed at creation | Grows automatically
Primitives | Yes, stored inline | No: boxed objects (Integer)
Type rules | Covariant, checked at runtime (ArrayStoreException) | Invariant, checked at compile time
Length | a.length field | list.size() method
API | Arrays helpers only | Full List API, streams, equals by content
Memory for 1M ints | About 4 MB | Roughly 4 to 5 times more (references plus Integer objects)
Rule of thumb: use ArrayList in business code and APIs. Use arrays for fixed-size primitive data in hot paths (buffers, matrices, counters), and for var-args. Convert with List.of(arr) or Arrays.asList(arr) for object arrays, and IntStream.of(arr).boxed().toList() for int[].
